modelResponse.episodeSummary: 82F with known AFib and heart failure presenting with symptomatic bradycardia (38 bpm) and toxic digoxin levels.
modelResponse.rhythm: Junctional escape rhythm (or slow regular bradycardia)
keyECGEvidence: preEventNote: Known AFib now with slow REGULAR response — suggests AV junctional takeover
modelResponse.mechanism: Digoxin-induced inhibition of the AV node and increased refractory periods, leading to failure of atrial impulse conduction and subsequent junctional escape.
contributingFactors: potassium: 5.6 mmol/L HIGH (hyperkalemia increases digoxin sensitivity)
creatinine: 2.1 mg/dL HIGH (acute on CKD reduces drug clearance)
History of Heart Failure and CKD stage 3

rejectedAlternatives.why: pWavePresent: false and clinical history of AFib with sudden regular slow response suggests non-sinus origin.
While the rate is slow, the primary driver is the confirmed toxic digoxin level and characteristic 'scooped' ST segments.

recommendedActions: Immediate bedside assessment of hemodynamic stability and pulse quality.
Notify attending physician and cardiology team immediately.
Administer potassium-lowering therapy if indicated by clinical status (consultation required due to hyperkalemia).
Hold all further doses of Digoxin.
Consider administration of calcium gluconate/chloride if severe hyperkalemia or symptomatic toxicity is suspected.
Monitor for worsening of nausea, vomiting, and visual disturbances.
Maintain hydration status and monitor urine output closely.
uncertainty: Exact AV block degree cannot be fully determined without a continuous 12-lead ECG strip to visualize the relationship between P-waves (if any) and QRS complexes.
